Quantum Field Theory and the Volume Conjecture
Tudor Dimofte and Sergei Gukov
California Institute of Technology 452-48, Pasadena, CA 91125
The volume conjecture states that for a hyperbolic knot K in the three-sphere S3
the asymptotic growth of the colored Jones polynomial of K is governed by the hy-
perbolic volume of the knot complement S3\K. The conjecture relates two topological
invariants, one combinatorial and one geometric, in a very nonobvious, nontrivial man-
ner. The goal of the present lectures∗is to review the original statement of the volume

The many dimensions of the volume conjecture
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:gen label="sec:gen"}

There are several natural ways in which one might try to generalize the basic volume conjecture [\[VC\]](#VC){reference-type="eqref" reference="VC"}. One possibility is to consider not just $k=N$ (or $q=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{N}}$), but arbitrary values of $k$ (or $q$). Another option would be to ask what happens to subleading terms in the asymptotic expansion of $V_N(K;q)$ as $N\to\infty$. blocks.title: Parametrized VC
blocks.content:
The original volume conjecture only held for a special root of unity $q = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{N}}$. In order to generalize to arbitrary $q=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{k}}$, the appropriate limit to consider is

$$k\to\infty\,,\qquad N\to\infty\,,\qquad u := i\pi\frac { N} k \quad\text{fixed}\, \label{lim}$$

(or $q\to 1$, $q^N = e^{2u}$ fixed). The question, then, is how to understand

$$\lim_{k,N\to\infty} J_N(K;q)^{1/k}\quad ?$$

blocks.title: Quantum VC
blocks.content:
The second option for generalizing the volume conjecture [\[VC\]](#VC){reference-type="eqref" reference="VC"} is to ask for higher-order terms in the asymptotic expansion of the colored Jones polynomial. Let us define a new "quantum" parameter $\hbar$ as

$$\hbar = \frac{i\pi}{k}\,,$$

so that

$$q = e^{2\hbar}\,.$$

blocks.title: Groups and representations
Links and 3-manifolds
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:links label="sec:links"}

The final generalization of the volume conjecture that we consider is to arbitrary links in arbitrary three-manifolds. Here we really begin to require a true TQFT description of the "quantum $G$-invariants" of knots and links. This was supplied by quantum Chern-Simons theory with compact gauge group $G$ in [@Wit-Jones], and reinterpreted via quantum groups and R-matrices in [@Resh-Tur]. Cutting and gluing
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:cut label="sec:cut"}

In its more mathematical incarnation, a 3-dimensional TQFT can be thought of as a functor $Z$ that assigns

$$\begin{array}{c@{\qquad}c@{\qquad}c}
 \text{closed 3-manifold $M$} & \leadsto & \text{number $Z(M)$} \\
 \text{closed 2-manifold $\Sigma$} &\leadsto & \text{vector space $Z(\Sigma)$} \\
 \text{closed 1-manifold $S^1$} &\leadsto & \text{category $Z(S^1)$} \\
 \text{point $p$} &\leadsto & \text{2-category $Z(p)$}\,.
\end{array}$$

blocks.title: Quantization
Methods
blocks.content:
The problem of quantization can be approached in many different ways. Each approach has its advantages and disadvantages, but in the end all methods are expected to yield the same result. blocks.title: Quantization of Chern-Simons theory
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:TQFT_CS label="sec:TQFT_CS"}

Consider Chern-Simons theory with gauge group $G$ --- either compact or complex --- on a knot complement $M = \widetilde{M}\backslash K$, with $\partial M = T^2$. The phase space ${\cal M}$ associated to $T^2$ is simply the space of flat $G$-connections on $T^2$, modulo gauge equivalence. Since a flat connection is completely determined by the conjugacy classes of its holonomies, we have

$$\begin{aligned}
 {\cal M}&= {\cal M}_{{\rm flat}} (G;T^2) \\
 &= \left\{ \text{representations :}\;\;\pi_1(T^2)\to G \right\}/\text{conjugation}\,.
\end{aligned}$$
